optimizer_switches.name: materialization
optimizer_switches.explanation: A subquery or derived table is executed once and its result stored in a temporary table for reuse. It may spill to disk past tmp_table_size (MySQL's TempTable engine) or the smaller of tmp_table_size and max_heap_table_size (MEMORY engine, MariaDB).

warnings.text: 1 temp table(s) (Materialize) — up to 5 rows; may spill to disk
1 sort operation(s) — 5 rows; may use disk-based filesort
Filesort detected with sort_buffer_size=256.0 KB. Whether it spills depends on the sort's row count and record size.
Query materializes 1 temp table(s); tmp_table_size is 16.0 MB. This limit alone does not show whether a table spilled to disk.

suggestions.action: Check internal_tmp_mem_storage_engine and temporary-table disk usage before raising tmp_table_size.
suggestions.why: the default TempTable engine limits each in-memory internal temporary table by tmp_table_size, and max_heap_table_size does not apply to it; only the MEMORY engine also uses max_heap_table_size, taking the smaller of the two. A temporary table in the plan does not by itself show that it spilled to disk.

suggestions.action: Increase sort_buffer_size or add an ordered index to avoid filesort
Check sort merge passes and query timing before increasing sort_buffer_size for this session.
suggestions.why: when sort records exceed the buffer, MySQL can write sorted runs and merge them. A larger buffer may avoid that work; small sorts may already fit in memory. Test session-level changes and account for concurrent sorting sessions before changing the global default.

suggestions.action: Check the internal temporary-table engine and disk usage before increasing tmp_table_size for this session.
suggestions.why: MySQL 8.0.28+ TempTable uses tmp_table_size as its per-table limit; max_heap_table_size does not limit TempTable. Shared TempTable RAM and mmap limits also affect disk usage. If the internal engine is MEMORY, the smaller of tmp_table_size and max_heap_table_size applies instead.

executive_summary: Query materializes 1 temp table and sorts the result; examines ~3,000 rows to return 5 in 3.6 ms. Main finding: the sort will likely spill to disk because sort_buffer_size is too small.

complexity.rationale: Filesort: MySQL sorts the output in the server layer. Priority-queue filesort (LIMIT) is not detected today — we report the upper bound.
Full table scan: the storage engine returns every row; cost scales with the table size.

complexity.big_o: build: O(n)  •  scan: O(1) per probe, O(rows) to fetch all
complexity.rationale: Materialize is a two-phase operator. The build pays the inner subquery's cost ONCE; each scan of the temp table is effectively constant time. Don't compound build cost by loops.

build_complexity.rationale: Streaming aggregation: reads each input row once and updates the aggregate values. Any input sorting is a separate child operator with its own cost.

scan_complexity.big_o: O(1) per probe, O(rows) to fetch all
scan_complexity.rationale: Materialize scan: reads the pre-computed temp table. Each probe is constant time once the table is in memory.

complexity.rationale: Streaming aggregation: reads each input row once and updates the aggregate values. Any input sorting is a separate child operator with its own cost.
Index scan: reads every entry of the index in key order. Cheaper than a table scan because the index is smaller, but still O(n).
